outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, refined for eloquence and flow while preserving all original imagery and meaning:

---

Startled from its snow-day slumber by a neighbor's mutt, it struck its buzzard's head and, wings nearly too broad for the descent it had planned, could not solve the tangle of the white pine's limbs. Somewhere an awkward angel knows whether it was dead before it struck the ground. Any sinner could tell it was dead after—eyes vanished beneath bare, wrinkled lids, feet drawn up nearly to its hands. I had loved watching thistle and millet disappear beneath it in the yard. As snow settles over feathers that will still gleam iridescent come spring, I find myself remembering a businessman who once drew a dripping handful of pocket change and flung it down a subway grate beside a homeless man. The coins clattered and bounced, vanishing into the humid dark. *Now you're having a shitty day too,* the rich man said. But this is not a shitty day, nor will it be, when I lift the bird—its toes curling stiff within a shopping bag—and carry it to a houseless scrap of oak savannah, the very ground from which its birdseed came, and press it into the deeper snow, so that what one man hoarded might, by the thaw, be given back.

---

**Key refinements made:**
- Smoothed transitions between clauses for better readability
- Adjusted verb tenses for consistency (e.g., "had loved" to mark the memory as past)
- Added italics to set off the businessman's dialogue, clarifying voice
- Tightened phrasing (e.g., "settles over" instead of "covers," "gleam iridescent" instead of "be iridescent") for more vivid, active imagery
- Clarified the final image's cause-and-effect logic ("the very ground from which its birdseed came") for smoother narrative flow
- Preserved the stark, elegiac tone and all factual/narrative details from your original piece

Roused mid-hibernation on a snowbound afternoon by the neighbor's dog, the creature struck its vulture-like skull and found itself unable to navigate the white pine's branches, its wingspan too generous for the landing it had intended. Some clumsy angel alone knows whether death arrived before impact. Any sinner, though, could confirm it afterward—lids closed and creased over invisible eyes, talons curled nearly to meet its feet.

I used to relish watching it clear thistle and millet seed from beneath itself in my yard. Now, as snow blankets plumage destined to gleam again come spring, I find myself recalling a scene: a well-dressed man emptying a fistful of damp coins down a subway grate near a man without shelter. The change rattled and echoed as it fell, swallowed by the humid darkness below. "There," the wealthy man said, "now your day's ruined too."

Except my day isn't ruined, nor will it be when I lift the bird—its rigid toes curling inside a shopping bag—and carry it to an unclaimed stretch of oak savannah, the very patch whose scattered seed had lured it here. I'll bury it in the deeper drifts, so that what one man clutched to himself might, come the thaw, be returned to the world.

# The Buzzard

It must have happened sometime before dawn. Startled from sleep by the neighbor's dog—barking at some shadow, some passing car, some private canine grievance—the buzzard bolted upward in the darkness, disoriented, and struck its head against something in its panicked ascent. Whether it died in that instant or in the moments after, tumbling downward into the waiting branches of the white pine, I cannot say. What I know is that it became entangled there, its wings caught in the needled lattice, and that by morning it hung suspended between earth and sky, already stiff, already gone.

I found it in the yard where the snow was beginning to gather, its features hardened into that particular rigidity that death imposes on a body—the eyes clouded, the talons curled inward as if still gripping some perch that no longer existed. I stood there longer than I meant to. This was the same spot where I used to watch it visit the feeder, dipping its head toward the thistle and millet seed I'd scattered for the smaller birds, tolerated by them in some unspoken truce. There had been a strange pleasure in observing this larger, wilder creature partake in something so domestic, so deliberately provided. Now it lay still, and the snow was starting to fall around it in earnest.

The snow falling reminded me, unaccountably, of something I'd witnessed months earlier in the city—a memory that surfaced now with unwelcome clarity. I had been walking near a subway grate when I saw a man in an expensive coat pause before a homeless man huddled against the cold. The businessman reached into his pocket and withdrew a handful of change, then flung it down through the grate, watching it scatter and vanish into the darkness below, out of reach. He laughed as he did it. "Now you're having a shitty day too," he said, and walked on, satisfied with his cruelty, as though misfortune were a game he'd just won.

I think of that moment now, standing over the frozen bird, and I find myself silently arguing with the businessman's words, months too late for him to hear it. It was not, I insist, a shitty day. Not really. Not in the way he meant it—as some universal currency of suffering, doled out and mocked in equal measure. There is a difference between cruelty performed for sport and the plain, indifferent tragedy of a startled bird and a low-hanging branch. The world does not owe us its meaning, and not every hardship is a punishment or a joke.

So I have decided what to do with the buzzard. I will carry it—carefully, respectfully—to the wild oak savannah at the edge of the property, where the snow drifts deep and undisturbed beneath the old trees. I will bury it there, beneath the accumulating white, and let it rest through the winter. There is something fitting in this: the seed I once hoarded and offered only sparingly, thistle and millet doled out at my own discretion, will now return to the wider world entire. By the time the thaw comes in spring, the ground will take back what I once contained in feeders and small rituals of feeding. The fox, the insects, the soil itself—all of it will have its share. What was once mine to give will simply become the world's again, redistributed without ceremony, the way it was always meant to be.

# What the Snow Keeps

The bird had been resting in the crook of a white pine's lower branches, tucked against the trunk the way small things learn to tuck themselves against the cold—finding the one place where bark breaks wind, where old needles cluster thick enough to hold a little borrowed warmth. It was a snow day, the kind that empties streets and silences the usual clatter of engines and voices, leaving only the hush of accumulation. I don't know what startled it. Perhaps only my footsteps, muffled as they were, arriving too suddenly in a world grown unused to sound. It burst upward in that frantic, blind way birds do when fear outpaces navigation, and it struck the trunk—not a branch, not a soft landing, but the hard vertical face of the tree itself—and dropped.

I stood there for a long moment before I understood what I'd witnessed. The bird lay small and still in the snow, its wings arranged by gravity into something almost peaceful, almost deliberate, though I knew there was nothing deliberate in it at all. Just panic, then impact, then this.

I thought, unbidden, of a man I'd once watched on a downtown sidewalk—a businessman in a wool coat that cost more than most people's rent, who paused beside a homeless man holding out a paper cup, and instead of dropping coins into the cup, tossed them onto the pavement beside it. Not into his hands. Not into his cup. Beside him, so that the man had to bend, had to scrape at frozen concrete, had to perform his need publicly while the businessman walked on, already checking his phone, already forgetting. I remember thinking at the time that this was a particular kind of cruelty—not the cruelty of refusal, which at least respects a boundary, but the cruelty of almost-giving, of turning generosity into a small theater of humiliation. He wanted to be seen giving without the discomfort of contact. He wanted the homeless man's degradation as much as his gratitude, maybe more.

I don't know why the bird summoned that memory. Maybe only because both were small deaths of a kind—one literal, one a slow erosion of dignity—that occurred because something more powerful moved carelessly through a world it did not bother to consider. The businessman never looked back to see the coins scattered on the concrete. I doubt he thought of that man again before he reached the end of the block. The bird, too, was collateral: my footsteps, someone else's rhythm, ended a life that had only wanted to survive the storm in the shelter it had found.

I could have left the bird where it fell. This is, after all, the ordinary math of winter—small things die, snow covers them, spring reveals what's left. But I found that I didn't want to leave it to chance the way the businessman had left that man to scrape at frozen ground. I wanted, instead, to do something that mattered, even if the something was small, even if no one would ever know or care that I'd done it.

So I dug a shallow hollow in the snow beneath the pine, in the savannah stretch of open ground where I'd scattered birdseed earlier that same morning, before the world went quiet and white. I laid the bird's body there, among the black oil sunflower seeds and the cracked corn, in the snow that would, in a few months, begin to soften and give way to thaw. I thought about how the ground under that spot would eventually receive both the seed and the small bird together, how what had been a startled, ended life might feed the soil that fed the seeds that fed the next generation of birds who would land in that same pine, tuck themselves into that same crook of branches, survive one more winter because something had gone back into the ground instead of simply being forgotten.

It wasn't much. I understood that. Burying a bird in birdseed is not a redistribution of wealth, is not justice, does not undo the small daily cruelties that pass for interaction in a world grown careless with its own power. But it felt, in that moment, like a refusal—a small and deliberate counter-gesture to the coins tossed carelessly onto concrete, to the callousness that takes pleasure in almost-giving. I wanted to give the bird something whole. I wanted its death to mean something beyond the accident of my footsteps, to become, instead of an ending, a kind of unglamorous continuation.

By spring, the snow would melt and carry what nutrients it could down into that patch of savannah ground. The bird would become part of what fed the very species it had once belonged to. And I would remember, each time I saw birds gathering there among the reemerging grass, that meaning is not something we find lying around, already made—it's something we insist on making, snowbank by frozen snowbank, gesture by quiet gesture, even when no one else is watching, even when the making feels almost too small to matter.

Because it isn't, I think, too small. Because someone has to be the version of humanity that buries the bird with care instead of dropping coins beside a beggar's hand. Because the world will keep offering us both kinds of moments—the careless cruelty and the chance to answer it—and what we do in that narrow, snow-quiet space between them is the only measure we really have of who we've decided to become.

**Somewhere in the Quiet**

She was startled awake by a sound she couldn't place—not quite a knock, not quite a whisper, but something in between that seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere at once. The clock read 3:17 AM, that strange hour when the world feels suspended between one day and the next.

She lay still, listening, wondering if the sound had come from somewhere inside the house or from the storm building outside. Any explanation seemed plausible in the darkness: a branch against the window, the house settling, or simply her mind conjuring noise from silence.

She thought about how easily we startle awake—not just from sound, but from memory, from sudden realization, from the small shocks life delivers when we least expect them. We spend so much of our lives believing we are anchored somewhere solid, only to discover that any sense of certainty can dissolve in an instant.

The wind picked up outside, rattling the old windowpane, and she finally understood. Just wind. Just an old house breathing in the night. She settled back into her pillow, but sleep remained somewhere just out of reach, hovering at the edge of consciousness.

Perhaps that's what those startling moments teach us—that any comfort we find is temporary, that home is not a fixed point but the way we return to stillness after being unsettled. Somewhere between fear and relief, she drifted off again, the house quiet once more, holding its secrets until the next unexpected sound broke through the dark.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about finding a dead bird in the snow that unexpectedly triggers a memory of witnessing a cruel act of "charity" toward a homeless man, ending with an act of quiet redemption.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Snow Kept

I found it near the hedge, wings folded like a letter no one would read—a small weight against the white, its eye already gone to glass. Something in the stillness pulled a thread in me, and I was twelve again, standing outside the church where a man named Otis slept in the doorway, his cart of cans arranged like a modest inheritance.

I remember the woman in the good coat who stopped, who smiled the smile of someone about to be photographed, who held out a sandwich until he reached for it—then pulled it back an inch, laughing, "Say please properly," while her friend recorded it for something, for someone, for the currency of having been seen being kind. Otis said please. He said it twice. The word came out of him like something already worn thin from use, and she gave it to him then, satisfied, already walking away before he'd finished thanking her, because the thanking was never really the point.

I didn't do anything. I was twelve. I told myself that for years—the sentence a small stone I kept in my pocket, worn smooth from handling.

Now, at the hedge, I crouch down. The bird is nothing—sparrow, maybe, its feet curled inward like a question it stopped asking. But I find myself gathering it anyway, this small failure of the sky, cradling it in my bare hands though the cold bites at my knuckles. I carry it to the base of the oak where the ground is soft with old leaves beneath the snow's crust, and I dig with a stick, then my fingers, until there's a space enough for it.

I don't pray. I don't have the right words for that. I just place it in the dark earth and cover it, patting the snow back over like tucking in something that can no longer feel the tucking.

It isn't Otis. It isn't the sandwich, or the twelve-year-old who said nothing, or the woman who mistook humiliation for generosity. It's just a bird, and my hands are just hands, doing this one small thing because the world asked nothing of me and I decided to answer anyway.

The snow keeps falling, unbothered, indifferent to my small ceremony. But somewhere in this quiet act—unwitnessed, unrecorded, needing no permission and expecting no thanks—something old and stone-worn in my pocket grows lighter.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short literary reflection on mortality and generosity, weaving together the death of a backyard bird and a memory of a rich man mocking a homeless person, ending with the speaker burying birdseed in snow as an act of grace.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Snow Keeps

The sparrow died the way small things often do—quietly, and near a window, so that someone would have to notice. I found it in the blue hour before the sun committed to rising, its body already stiffened into a comma, as if the last thing it wrote was a pause, not an ending. The feeder above it still swung slightly, indifferent, dispensing seed to whoever came next.

I thought, absurdly, of a man in a camel-hair coat I once watched step around a woman sleeping in a doorway on Lexington Avenue. He didn't just avoid her—he performed his avoidance, lifting his polished shoes with theatrical delicacy, muttering something to his companion that made them both laugh. The cold that morning was the kind that makes your bones announce themselves. She had a sign, cardboard, soft with old rain: *anything helps*. He had everything, and gave nothing, and found her circumstance amusing in the particular way that only the insulated can.

I don't know why these two moments have nested together in me, the bird and the man, but I suspect it's this: both scenes are about what falls through the gaps we allow. The sparrow fell through the gap between abundance and access—there was seed, there was shelter, but not enough, not in time. The woman fell through a gap made not by scarcity but by choice, by a man who had more than enough warmth and chose instead to be entertained by her lack of it.

Mortality doesn't discriminate, but generosity does. We choose, constantly, who gets to be a fellow creature and who gets to be scenery.

So this is what I do, small and probably useless: I go out into the snow with a bag of seed and I don't just scatter it—I bury it, pushing my bare fingers into the cold crust, making little pockets so the wind won't steal it before the birds wake. My hands ache. Good. Let them ache. Let this be a kind of penance for the man in the camel-hair coat, for every gap I have personally allowed something to fall through, for every doorway I have walked past with my eyes already elsewhere.

The snow will melt eventually and expose these small buried gifts to whoever is hungry enough to look. This is not much of a redemption. But grace was never about the size of the gesture—only about the decision, made again and again, to notice the cold and answer it with something warm, however small, however late.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental narrative fragment—part elegy, part social commentary—about discovering a dead bird after a storm, incorporating themes of hoarding, charity, and seasonal renewal.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. What the Storm Left**

The bird lay on the sidewalk like punctuation at the end of a sentence no one had finished writing. Rain-slicked, wing bent at the wrong angle, its small body already stiffening in the gray hour after the storm broke. I almost stepped over it. This is what we do with the dead now—step over, step around, keep walking toward whatever errand justified leaving the house.

But the neighborhood was full of debris that morning: shingles peeled back like old scabs, a lawn chair three yards from where it belonged, someone's charity donation bin knocked sideways, spilling coats and cracked dishware onto the wet grass. Abundance, overturned. Someone had given away too much or too little, and now it lay exposed to weather, undifferentiated from trash.

**II. Inventory**

My grandmother kept every twist-tie that ever sealed a bread bag. Drawers of them, coiled like small dead insects, sorted by nothing except the fact of their preservation. She said: *you never know*. She said: *waste not*. She died in a house so full of just-in-case that the paramedics had to angle the stretcher sideways through hallways lined with folded grocery bags, inside more folded grocery bags, inside boxes she'd saved from Christmases decades gone.

I think about her when I see the bird. The impulse to gather, to keep, to make useful what has already stopped being anything but itself.

The donation bin: someone's excess becoming someone else's want, except now it's just wet wool and rusting hinges. Charity requires this constant motion—things must keep moving through hands, or they curdle into hoard, into landfill, into the particular grief of unopened mail addressed to the deceased.

**III. Small Body, Necessary Weight**

I did not step over the bird. I don't know why this one, this ordinary sparrow or wren, when I have stepped over a hundred like it. Perhaps because the storm had just passed and everything felt suddenly accountable—the trees down, the power out on Fifth Street, the whole neighborhood doing math about what could be salvaged and what was simply gone.

I used a broken shingle as a shovel. I made a small grave in the mud at the base of an oak that had lost half its crown to the wind. This is not efficient. This is not what you do with sparrows. There are, in this city alone, some four hundred thousand small deaths a year from window-strikes, from storms, from the ten thousand ordinary violences of infrastructure—and I cannot bury them all, cannot even find most of them, and yet.

**IV. Renewal, or the Argument For It**

Spring insists on itself regardless. Three days after the storm the crocuses came up through the storm-wrack like they hadn't heard the news. The downed oak, or what remained standing of it, would push new growth from its wound come April—trees do this, this stubborn insurgency of green from injury.

The donation bin got righted by someone, eventually. The coats went somewhere—a shelter, a resale shop, a stranger's shoulders against next winter's cold. The twist-ties, after my grandmother's funeral, went into a single garbage bag that took four of us to carry, and none of us said what we were thinking, which was: *this was not a hoard of things but a hoard of moments she couldn't bear to let become the past.*

**V. Elegy, Brief**

Small bird, I did not know you. I know only that the storm took something from the sky and gave it to the ground, the way storms do, the way years do, the way charity and hoarding are both just different names for what we do with what we cannot bear to lose—give it away, or keep it forever, as if either could undo the fact of ending.

The mud has already closed over where I buried you. By June there will be grass there indistinguishable from any other grass. This is, I have come to think, the whole difficult argument of spring: that renewal doesn't erase the losses underneath it, only grows, patient and green, directly out of them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic vignette in dense, run-on prose style about the death of a wild bird outside one's home, interspersed with a disturbing memory of wealth disparity, culminating in a symbolic gesture of redistribution.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Sparrow Knew

The bird fell against the window at 6:14 in the morning, a small thud like a knuckle on wood, and by the time I reached the glass it was already lying on its back in the gravel, wings folded wrong, one eye open to the white sky as if still counting the seconds of its flight, and I stood there in my socks on the cold porch thinking of nothing, thinking of everything, thinking of the man I saw once through the tinted window of a car so long it seemed to bend the street around itself, his hand resting on a dog whose collar cost more than my mother's monthly wage, and how he did not see the children pressed against the chain-link fence of the school lot, did not see them because seeing costs something too, and the bird's chest was still warm when I lifted it, feather-light, lighter than any of this, lighter than the guilt that gathers like static before rain, and I remembered the woman I'd watched counting coins at the register while behind her a boy in a coat that cost more than her rent scrolled his phone without looking up, the two of them occupying the same six feet of air as if the world had not decided, long ago, whose weight would bend the floor, and the bird did not know any of this, the bird only knew sky and then glass and then nothing, and I carried it to the garden where the frost had not yet let go of the grass, and I dug with my bare hands because I did not want metal between me and this small death, and I thought of the dog's collar again, the diamond stitching, the child's coat, the coins, and I laid the bird in the earth and covered it and then—because grief demands a gesture, because the hands must do something the mind cannot—I went inside and emptied my wallet into an envelope, all of it, the twenties and the ones and the coins that had been rattling loose for weeks, and left it on the porch of the family two doors down who share one car between four jobs, no note, no name, just the weight of it against their door before the sun was fully up, before anyone could refuse, before the sky could take anything else from anyone that morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
